name: Emerging-market stress
summary: Bank Indonesia raised rates to 6% on 18 Nov to support the rupiah near record lows; no EM default or IMF rescue
state: Bank Indonesia unexpectedly raised its benchmark rate by 0.25 points to 6% on 18 Nov after stepping up intervention, and the rupiah firmed to about 18,230 per dollar after touching a record near 18,290 on 17 Nov (Trading Economics). The currency had weakened to about 18,265 on 16 Nov (Databoks) amid Fed rate-rise bets and political uncertainty (The Jakarta Post). It has not fallen 10% in a month, and no major emerging economy in default, under capital controls or seeking emergency IMF support was found as of 19 Nov.
for_you: Pressure is concentrated in a few emerging-market currencies as US rates rise. It mainly affects investors and firms with exposure to those markets; travellers may see weaker local currencies.
rubric_hit: Normal: no major EM currency down >10% in a month, no default, capital controls or emergency IMF request

why: Energy-importing and heavily indebted emerging economies crack first in oil shocks and strong-dollar periods, with knock-on defaults and unrest.
drivers: Oil and food import bills, dollar strength, FX reserves, debt maturities, IMF programmes.

rubric.alert: A sovereign default or capital controls in a major emerging economy, or several in crisis at once.
rubric.watch: A major emerging economy's currency falls more than 10% in a month, its reserves fall fast, or it seeks emergency IMF support.
rubric.normal: No major emerging economy in acute currency or debt distress.
